title: Work as worship
hookLine: no one eats better food than what he earns with his own hands (Bukhari)
tomorrow: the rain wasn't his fault. so why call it cheating?

lines: RINGS OF IRON, ONE BY ONE.
cards: A first shift. An apron that doesn't fit yet, a register that beeps at you, a manager who says the coffee has to be right every time. It can feel like the opposite of anything holy.
Now a different workroom. A king sits at a bench, and he isn't signing laws. He's linking rings of iron, one into the next, measuring each one, making a coat of mail by hand.
He could have anything in the kingdom brought to him. He eats from this instead.

teach.b: The king is David. The Qur'an says God gave him grace, and in Pickthall's words, "We made the iron supple unto him," telling him to make coats of mail and measure the links, and to do right.

teach.h: THE SAME DAVID OF THE PSALMS.
teach.b: It's the same David Jews and Christians know as a singer of psalms; the Qur'an says he was given the Zabur, the Psalms. And here's why a king with a workbench matters.

teach.h: NO BETTER FOOD THAN YOUR OWN WORK.
teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says no one has ever eaten better food than what he eats from the work of his own hands, and that the Prophet of God, David, used to eat from the work of his hands.
Of all the examples he could have picked, he picked a king doing a craftsman's job. So work isn't the thing you do between acts of worship.
Done honestly, done well, with God in mind, it can be one. The measured link. The fair price.
The coffee made right when nobody's checking.
One to tell a friend tonight: the Prophet's example of the best food came from a king's hands, not his treasury.

how: Muslims are taught to earn a lawful living with their own effort; many begin work with Bismillah and treat honest, careful work, with a good intention, as part of their worship.

o: unpaid volunteering only, never a paid position
honest work, done well, counted as an act of worship
time spent at the masjid instead of going to a job

games.q: the king at the workbench — tap the pairs.
p: a king who ate from his own work

s: in Islam, a job is a worldly thing kept apart from worship
the Prophet said no one eats better food than what he earns with his own hands.
the Prophet's example of earning by hand was a king
David, who ate from the work of his own hands.
the Qur'an mentions David making coats of mail
34:10–11: the iron made supple; make coats of mail and measure the links.

games.q: your friend is closing at the café. the manager's gone, the floor is half-mopped, and her shift ends in five minutes. what fits honest hands?
o: finish the floor properly, even unseen; the work is part of what's honest.
clock out on time and leave a note; the hours are what she's paid for.
stay an hour unpaid to deep-clean everything; worship means going far beyond.
games.why: David measured every link. honest hands means the work itself is done right, not just the hours logged, and not a show of extra either.

practice: Pick one small task within reach that you'd usually rush: a dish, a reply, a drawer. Do it now, slowly and properly, as if it were a link in David's coat. Then rest your hands, open, on your knees for the remaining time.

wordCard.voice: Work as worship: honest work, done well, counted as more than a paycheck. A king at a workbench is the example.

orig.note: Arabic: work, a deed; the same word is used for a person's deeds before God.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: honest hands, a king's habit on an ordinary shift. Work and money, begun.

sources.q: We made the iron supple unto him
